title: Design a microservice to handle uploading large files (100MB+) under high concurrency (streaming, presigned URLs, async metadata queue, reactive WebFlux, backpressure/rate limiting).
shortTitle: Design a microservice to handle uploading large files (100MB+) under high concurrency
keyPoints: Never buffer a large file in memory: a naive MultipartFile.getBytes() causes OutOfMemoryError under concurrency.
Presigned URLs let the client upload directly to S3 while the API handles only lightweight control-plane JSON.
S3 multipart upload splits files into independently retryable parts for resumability and parallel upload.
Metadata and processing (virus scan, thumbnails) happen asynchronously through a message queue.
Reactive WebFlux with Flux<DataBuffer> streams bytes without loading the whole file, using backpressure.
A per-user token-bucket rate limit prevents abuse and controls storage cost.
Validate the real MIME type from magic bytes, not the file extension, and virus-scan before marking usable.

s1_definition.oneliner: Do not move big bytes through your server; mint a presigned URL so the client uploads straight to object storage, and handle only lightweight metadata asynchronously on a non-blocking stack.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **No buffering** – Never load the entire file into heap memory; a hundred concurrent 100 MB uploads is 10 GB of heap, which is instant OutOfMemoryError.
- **Presigned URLs** – Object storage issues a short-lived, signed URL so the client uploads directly to S3; your API handles only tiny JSON.
- **Multipart upload** – For multi-gigabyte files, S3 multipart splits the file into independently uploadable and retryable parts.
- **Async processing** – Virus scan, MIME validation, and thumbnailing happen off the upload path via a message queue.
- **Reactive stack** – Spring WebFlux with `Flux<DataBuffer>` streams bytes without holding the whole file in memory, with backpressure.
s1_definition.analogy: Customers of National Bank of India need to upload large scanned loan files. Imagine the branch clerk personally carrying every customer's heavy suitcase into the vault. With one clerk and a thousand customers, the clerk collapses. Instead, the bank gives each customer a one-time pass (presigned URL) to drive their own suitcase straight to the warehouse (S3). The clerk only writes down "Rajesh dropped off suitcase 7 at 3pm" on a slip and puts it in an in-tray for later filing.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Designing a microservice for large file uploads under high concurrency starts with one principle: big bytes should never flow through the application server. At National Bank of India, customers like Rajesh upload 150 MB scanned property files during loan campaigns, thousands at once. A naive controller calling `getBytes()` caused OutOfMemoryError the moment a few hundred files arrived concurrently.

Pankaj's architecture uses presigned URLs: the client calls the API with just the filename and size, the API validates and mints a short-lived signed URL scoped to one S3 key, and the client uploads directly to S3. The server never touches the content. For multi-gigabyte KYC videos, S3 multipart upload splits the file into independently retryable parts. All heavy processing (virus scan, MIME magic-byte validation, thumbnail generation) happens asynchronously through a Kafka queue, decoupling the fast upload path from slow processing.

When bytes must flow through the service, reactive WebFlux with `Flux<DataBuffer>` streams chunks without holding the whole file in memory, and backpressure keeps memory bounded. A per-user token-bucket rate limit prevents one client from flooding storage bandwidth or cost. MIME type is validated from magic bytes, never from the extension, and untrusted content sits in a quarantine bucket until ClamAV clears it.

Remember one sentence: Keep the bytes off your server by minting presigned URLs, use multipart for very large files, handle metadata on a non-blocking reactive stack with backpressure, push processing onto an async queue, and validate magic bytes rather than trusting extensions.
